title: What School Readiness Really Means
hook: Being ready for school is less about reading early and more about social and emotional skills — following directions, taking turns, and managing feelings.
key_points: Self-regulation, listening, and getting along with others predict school success more than early academics.
Skills like separating from a parent, sharing, and handling frustration matter as much as letters and numbers.
Everyday routines, conversation, and play build these foundations naturally.
Readiness develops at different rates; reading and writing come later for many capable children.
content_html: Ask what "ready for school" means and many people picture a child who can already read. Child-development research points elsewhere: the strongest predictors of a smooth start to school are social and emotional — being able to follow directions, take turns, separate from a parent, and manage frustration without falling apart.
extra_html: Those skills don't need flashcards. They grow through everyday routines, back-and-forth conversation, and plenty of play. Academic skills like reading and writing tend to come later, and arrive at different times even for very capable children. Guidance like the CDC's positive-parenting tips for preschoolers frames readiness around these foundations rather than early academics. This is general educational information, not a developmental assessment.

related.title: Play Is How Young Children Learn
related.hook: For young children, play isn't a break from learning — it is the learning, building language, problem-solving, and social skills all at once.
